HEADLINE: Built's Marco Rossi's $15m hole in the ground
INTRO: For sale: one great big, stonking hole in the ground. Boasts incredible ocean views, in prime Sydney beach-side location. Asking price: $15 million.
TEXT:
For sale: one great big, stonking hole in the ground. Boasts incredible ocean views, in prime Sydney beach-side location. Asking price: $15 million.

If you needed further proof the Sydney real estate market has gone completely bonkers take a stroll along Tamarama Marine Drive where Marco Rossi - chairman and founder of the construction company Built - is flogging off a hole for a fortune (and when we say "hole" we are speaking literally, not figuratively).

Rossi bought the property back in 2007 for $11 million through the Blacket Agency, setting a record for the suburb at the time. He then went to the trouble of knocking down the existing building and excavating (at a cost of $1 million) - only to finally decide to move to Bellevue Hill instead, where he picked up the stately home Yoorami at the end of last year for $15 million.

Word is his partner, Stephanie Stokes, wanted the family to be closer to the school the couple's kids attend.

Whoever snaps up this Sydney real estate bargain will have the option of realising the plans which Rossi dreamt up, for which there is already development approval. Plans which include an eight-car garage, marble interiors and a lift from the street frontage up to the property. Plans which it is estimated will only cost another $7 mill to $8 mill to realise.

But you'd want to be quick. Given that chicken and fashion king Robbie Ingham flogged off his own Tamarama pile last week for an estimated $13.2 million, a hole in the ground of this quality, in this market, surely won't be around forever.

A hole! A hole! My kingdom for a hole!

HEADLINE: Tyrwhitt of Arabia, while Rex goes surfing
INTRO: One of the many wonderful things about reporting season is the stocktake you get to do of who's where and what they're all up to.
TEXT:
One of the many wonderful things about reporting season is the stocktake you get to do of who's where and what they're all up to.

Analysts were treated to a searing insight into the investment criteria of Ramsay Health on Tuesday's call with the company's famously loquacious chief executive, Chris Rex.

Famous for his laidback approach to these otherwise very serious phone hook-ups (and why wouldn't he be when he's returning double-digit growth?), Rex informed his audience of Ramsay's plans to build a new hospital in the Maldives. Where else?

"It's situated on a great surf break which probably doesn't generate many patients, but will probably require a significant amount of management time to ensure it is built properly. So ... Aloha!" he joked.

When asked, hopefully, by an interlocutor whether there might be a site visit, Rex quipped: "Maybe we can take this offline because it's a secret break and I don't want everybody to know."

Meanwhile, the release of results for the United Arab Emirates company Depa had the happy consequence of also revealing the latest career move of former Leightons CEO Hamish Tyrwhitt.

The Dubai-based firm - of which Tyrwhitt is now CEO - specialises in the "fit out and furnishing of five star hotels and resorts .. villas, palaces, private jets and yachts". A current project is the fit out of the presidential palace in Abu Dhabi. Which ought to suit his champagne tastes just perfectly.

It's been quite the heady whirl through pan-Asia to Arabia for Tyrwhitt. Only last year, we were reporting on how he had surfaced at Indonesia's Asia Resource Minerals after being unceremoniously flicked by the Leightons' (then) new Spanish owners.

HEADLINE: Google Australia headed for White Bay Power Station
INTRO: Technology giant Google might have had an original bid to redevelop the former White Bay Power Station on Sydney Harbour knocked back, but you don't take over the world by meekly accepting failure, do you?
TEXT:
Technology giant Google might have had an original bid to redevelop the former White Bay Power Station on Sydney Harbour knocked back, but you don't take over the world by meekly accepting failure, do you?

Google is expected to tell its Pyrmont-based staff on Tuesday that it is now negotiating directly with the UrbanGrowth NSW project, which Mike Baird has appointed as developer of the historic site, to base its Australian headquarters there. The negotiations could yet come to zilch, but the company seems pretty determined to us!

Google's presence (and no doubt enormous neon shingle) will ensure the emergence of a tech hub around them. Yes, White Bay will soon be the land of beards and mopeds and virgins in their late twenties.

Google currently occupies the Accenture building across the street from The Star casino complex, and multiple floors in Fairfax Media's building On Darling Island. Oh how we'll miss them…

HEADLINE: More checks on banks
TEXT:
The Turnbull government is contemplating further curbs on the banks in a bid to head off attempts by Labor to woo dissenting Coalition MPs into supporting a royal commission.

Sources have told The Australian Financial Review that later this week, when Labor is expected to move a motion in the House of Representatives calling for a royal commission on the banks, the government plans to counter with a motion of its own. Not only will it clarify the three steps it has taken in recently months to ward off a royal commission and placate the backbench, but it is planning to announce more measures.

Details are being kept secret, but sources said the measures would provide aggrieved bank consumers with an opportunity to immediately air their concerns or seek redress.

"It gives an opportunity for consumers to be heard while waiting for things to happen," said one person familiar with the details.

Already this year, the government has boosted the powers and resources of the regulator, the Australian Securities and Investments Commission. Then it announced that at least once a year bank executives would be required to appear before Parliament's house economics committee to explain such actions such as not passing on in full the Reserve Bank of Australia interest rate cuts. Most recently, Prime Minister Malcolm Turnbull and Treasurer Scott Morrison announced the government would establish a bank victims' tribunal as an alternative to long and financially crippling court action. The measures to be announced this week are believed to be in addition to the tribunal.

Like the tribunal, they stem from recommendations in a report in May issued by the Parliamentary Joint Committee on Corporations and Financial Services. "There will be immediate, interim and long-term measures," a source said.

The decision underscores growing sensitivity in the government over its threadbare majority and the potential for backbench dissent.

Several Coalition MPs, especially the Nationals, have been threatening to cross the floor in the lower house to support a royal commission unless the government implemented measures that had "teeth".

As the government was finalising its bank plans, Labor and the lower house crossbenchers were trying to outdo each other over same-sex marriage by giving notice that they would both introduce private member's bills to try to lure moderate Liberals into crossing the floor. But the big spot fire was in the Senate where there was a growing revolt over Section 18C of the Racial Discrimination Act.

In direct defiance of Mr Turnbull and Mr Morrison, both of whom have stressed that Section 18C cannot be a priority for the government while it is focused on budget repair, 13 of the 14 Coalition backbenchers in the Senate agreed to co-sponsor a private member's bill by Liberal senator Cory Bernardi.

The bill would remove "offend" and "insult" from the section which makes it illegal to "offend, insult, humiliate or intimidate another person or a group of people" on the basis of race or ethnicity. The following section, however, 18D, has exemptions for statements done "reasonably and in good faith" for academic, artistic or scientific purposes.

Former prime minister Tony Abbott attempted to repeal section 18c but backed off following a backlash from his backbench and ethnic communities.

Senator Bernardi also has the support of seven crossbench senators - Derryn Hinch, Bob Day, David Leyonhjelm and the four One Nation senators - but the bill cannot pass the Senate so long as Labor, the Greens and the Nick Xenophon Team remain opposed.

Nonetheless, the petition is a significant show of strength by the conservatives, which one Liberal said Mr Turnbull could not ignore forever.

At the ceremonial opening of Parliament on Tuesday, Labor leader Bill Shorten called on Mr Turnbull to support a motion reaffirming Parliament's "commitment to the right of all Australians to enjoy equal rights and be treated with equal respect regardless of race, colour, creed or origin, consistent with the Speaker's values".

In 1996, when Pauline Hanson first entered Parliament, then prime minister John Howard and opposition leader Kim Beazley co-operated to support an identical resolution.

"I believe this would be a powerful, bipartisan note to strike at the beginning of this term," Mr Shorten said.

As Senator Bernardi gathered his signatures, Mr Morrison again played down its import.

"It doesn't help me pay back one cent of debt, it doesn't help me reduce the deficit, it doesn't help me get one more person in a job, it doesn't help me get welfare under control, it doesn't help me improve the tax system. These are things I'm focused on," he said.

And he slammed Mr Shorten for "playing cheap politics" with the banks.

On either Wednesday or Thursday, Labor will move a motion in the House of Representatives calling for a royal commission on the banks.

Mr Shorten will also meet victims of bank scandals from NSW, Victoria and the ACT.

These will include representatives of the groups who continue to be affected by the collapse of Timbercorp and Great Southern, as well as a victims of more recent financial planning malpractice.

But Mr Morrison said Mr Shorten was not motivated by helping such people.

"Bill Shorten isn't motivated by supporting anyone's case or achieving anything positive in this space," the Treasurer said.

"He is just looking to pursue his own cynical political interest in all of this and to exploit people's legitimate concerns about issues in this area and trying to use them for his own political advantage. That's what Bill Shorten is doing.

"What he's proposing on a royal commission is only designed to pursue that objective.

"We've increased the resources of ASIC. In addition to that, we've ensured the transparency and accountability that will go with the regular appearances permanently of the banks joining both the RBA and APRA at regular appearances before the House of Representatives standing committee on economics. And in addition to that, we've initiated through the Ramsay Review in recent weeks the process to put in place a tribunal that will enable Australians to have a level playing field and have access to seeing their cases dealt with and addressed in a more meaningful way than currently occurs now."

Mr Morrison said the tribunal was a complicated proposal given there were already different tribunals dealing with superannuation and financial services.

He again accused Labor of ultimately threatening the economy by trying to weaken the banking sector.

"A strong banking and financial system was a, if not the, key reason why Australia withstood the financial storm of the GFC," he said.

"All that Bill Shorten is doing is undermining not only domestic confidence in our banking and financial system, but he raises questions in the international community, and in the international community they're asking what's wrong with Australia's banking and financial system?

"That is playing with fire and he should, frankly, not be so reckless and he should support the practical measures the government is implementing."

HEADLINE: MPs warned of new Silk Road agenda
TEXT:
Shanghai | Australia's new Parliament has been warned not to accept the argument from some sections of the business community pushing the economic benefits of China's Silk Road initiative, without recognising it as an attempt by Beijing to create a strategic bloc to counter the United States.

The Briefing Book, given to all MPs by the Parliamentary Library before Tuesday's opening of Parliament, provides a stark assessment of China's ambitions.

It singles out Beijing's plan to spend billions on infrastructure projects in the region, including in northern Australia, as an attempt to gain a strategic advantage and validate its claims over disputed waters in the South China Sea.

"As such, some see this initiative as a profound challenge to the current global political and economic status quo," said a briefing paper that was written by Geoff Wade from the Parliamentary Library.

Such a characterisation of China's Silk Road initiative, known as One Belt One Road (OBOR), is likely to anger Beijing, which has emphasised the trade benefits of improving infrastructure in the region.

Mr Wade has also highlighted growing tensions between some in the business community who favour greater engagement with China, and strategic analysts who are wary of Beijing's geopolitical ambitions.

"Business people are generally positive [about OBOR], while strategists have been less sanguine," said Mr Wade.

In her foreword to the Briefing Book, the head of the Parliamentary Library, Dianne Heriot, said the publication aimed to provide "snapshots of issues expected to figure during the Parliament's first months".

"The articles give a high-level perspective of key public policy issues," wrote Dr Heriot.

The Parliamentary Library is a research body for members of both Houses and is often relied upon by independent MPs and minor parties who don't have their own staff to cover all portfolio areas.

While OBOR was not a major issue during the recent federal election, China's growing strategic interests and soft power in Australia have become major headaches for the Turnbull government. The Australian Financial Review reported on Tuesday about how Chinese political donors in Australia will increasingly demand a greater say in public life.

Huang Xiangmo, the chairman of property developer Yuhu Group and a major donor himself, said the Chinese community has been used as a "cash cow" by Australian politicians and then ignored.

"We need to learn ... how to have a more efficient combination between political requests and political donations," he wrote in an editorial for the Global Times newspaper.

The warnings by Mr Wade about the strategic intentions behind China's new Silk Road come as Beijing has begun ramping up investments.

In the first quarter of this year, Chinese companies made $US3.59 billion ($4.75 billion) of investments into OBOR countries, including Singapore, India and Indonesia.

That is up more than 40 per cent from the year before, according to a report by law firm King & Wood Mallesons, which cited Chinese Ministry of Commerce figures.

"Within Australia, enterprises, banks and law firms are promoting the OBOR initiative as an economic opportunity for the country," Mr Wade wrote. "Despite the claimed economic nature of the OBOR agenda, critics see the initiative as being simultaneously a strategic program."

Mr Wade said that within China, the role of the People's Liberation Army in protecting this new infrastructure has been widely discussed.

"China clearly portrays OBOR as both being premised on and further validating China's claims to the islands of the South China Sea, while on the other side of the Indian Ocean, Djibouti is providing China with both a trade port as well as its first overseas military base."

The paper says Australia needs to keep a close watch on the progress of OBOR and adopt a "prudent attitude" in determining how the bilateral relationship develops.

"Broader concerns relate to the longer-term aims of China, with the possibility that the OBOR agenda is aimed at creating a Eurasia-wide, China-led bloc to counter the US."

If it lives up to its potential, OBOR will involve about 65 countries and Chinese investment of roughly $US1 trillion during the next 10 to 15 years.

It is the brainchild of President Xi Jinping, who in announcing it harked back to the glory days of the Silk Road era, a time when China was the centre of the world and boasted the world's largest economy.

It is also partly a response to China's excess industrial capacity, mainly in steel and cement, which would be able to be soaked up by building infrastructure in the region.

Mr Wade, who previously worked as an independent analyst, was largely responsible for raising strategic concerns about a long-term lease over the Port of Darwin being sold to a Chinese company.

HEADLINE: Canadians courted for fresh Ausgrid auction
TEXT:
The NSW government is going all out to get Canadian pension funds interested in electricity distributor Ausgrid to provide some competitive tension and avoid having to sell it off cheap.

As revealed by Street Talk on Tuesday, the state and its advisors, Deutsche Bank and UBS, have started scheduling meetings with investors in New York and Canada as it seeks to attract strong overseas competition to bidding consortia being put together in the local Australian market.

The emphasis being placed on North American suitors indicates that those parties are unlikely to bump up against the security issues that caused the last-minute collapse of the original auction for Ausgrid when both the final bidders - China's State Grid Corporation and Hong Kong-listed Cheung Kong Infrastructure - were ruled out by Federal Treasurer Scott Morrison.

While those two are still waiting in the wings hoping to salvage something from their bids and potentially link up with local parties to allow them to keep their respective interests below a set percentage that may be allowable, Street Talk understands those hopes may be misplaced. Indeed, sources say the NSW government would not have abandoned the previous Ausgrid process if it saw any way to restructure the two bids to arrive at an acceptable transaction. That signals that State Grid and CKI - or any Chinese-linked bidder - are effectively out of the picture for the auction re-run, which may not have any set limit on maximum foreign involvement.

The North American roadshow puts the spotlight on major infrastructure investors from that region that are expected to play a material role in the revamped sale process, which is expected to get under way in weeks.

The line-up is understood to include Borealis, Brookfield Asset Management and large Canadian pension funds, including Ontario Teachers' Pension Plan, Canada Pension Plan Investment Board, Alberta Investment Management Corp, British Columbia Investment Management Corporation and Public Sector Pension Investment Board.

HEADLINE: Spenceley phones a friend
TEXT:
It should come as no surprise that Tony Grist and James Spenceley are close.

The two telco founders were in the trenches together in what was one of the most unlikely victories in modern corporate history, scuttling TPG Telecom's attempts to stop a merger between Grist's Amcom and Spenceley's Vocus last year after David Teoh amassed a 19.9 per cent blocking stake in Amcom.

Just days after the launch of Spenceley's new funds management business, MHOR Asset Management, as revealed by The Australian Financial Review, Grist is about to sign up as the first high-profile investor.

Over last Wednesday and Thursday, Grist sold down close to $9.9 million worth of shares in Vocus. Those funds will be used for expanding his own venture capital business, Albion Capital Partners, as well as an investment in Spenceley's new fund.

The partnership between Grist and Spenceley has been fruitful for both parties. The two have a private deal with fixed wireless broadband provider Uniti Wireless and the first private company MHOR will invest in is Robo 3D, a California-based 3D printer manufacturer that Grist is bringing to the market. "I have great respect for James' management and leadership abilities ... we are firm friends," Grist said to Street Talk.
